'''

'''
Ok so here is my plan, I am going to implement it as a class and each of the behaviors is going to be a method. There will be a play method that moves between teh behaviors and it will have the control flow logic. 

Ex:
self.acceptLogs()
self.setInitialPosition()
self.getLogAtCurrentPosition()
type = self.getCurrentPositionType()
if type == "participant":
    participant self.getparticipantNameAndValue()
etc...


I am basically trying a new approach where I am structuring the program around the designs behaviors, then the mapping will be trivial. 

Anyway, I'm just going implement, iterate and keep refining my approach as I learn more of the nuances in this framework.
'''


'''
    A question for myself, if I am implementing the behaviors in functions, then why do I need to map the behaviors manually? I can automatically map the design onto the implementation and if I use the same variable name as the participant name, then I can automate that as well. 
'''

06239500-0a73-4c84-a295-c6e7ccb97c4c.name: note_on_nested_designs
06239500-0a73-4c84-a295-c6e7ccb97c4c.content:
'''
    Note:
    I need the control graph and the invariants to
    actually realize some of the behaviors, I will be 
    simulating it for now.

    However, this does raise a very interesting point
    for me. Lets say we are inside the behavior which
    enforces the invariant, I think that can be a design
    graph of its own. I can build in these abstractions
    which will make it very easy to manage. This graph
    will just need to know that the behavior enforce invariants
    is being exhibited as a behavior. What the means and the
    correctness of that can be defined in another design grpah.
    
    There will also be a very neat pattern where the inputs into
    the enforce invariant behavior will be its environment but that
    will come from this graph. It will setup a really neat pattern
    but I can't fully articulate it yet.

    Its actually a very very cool pattern if you think about it,
    every single design is part of a bigger design. Every design
    tries to regulate the environment which it allows into its
    reality so that its reality remains semantically valid. 
    However, that environment comes from another design, so in this
    sense, invariants are how designs become aware of each other.

    Its like a nested reality, there is nothing special about
    each level, its not like its higher or lower, its just about
    what is the environment that a design lives in. A design is nested
    if its environment is created by another design.    
'''
